standards.title: HTTP Datagrams and the Capsule Protocol

requirements.summary: HTTP Datagrams are sent only for a request whose extension semantics explicitly authorize them.
A Datagram for an existing request without known Datagram semantics terminates that request rather than the connection.
HTTP/3 aborts only the existing unassociated request stream with H3_DATAGRAM_ERROR 0x33.
A Quarter Stream ID above 2^60-1 is an HTTP/3 connection error of H3_DATAGRAM_ERROR 0x33.
A QUIC DATAGRAM payload too short to decode a Quarter Stream ID is H3_DATAGRAM_ERROR 0x33.
An HTTP/3 Datagram is not sent after its associated stream send side has closed.
An HTTP/3 Datagram received after the associated receive side closes is silently dropped.
A Datagram naming a request stream not created yet is silently dropped under the selected RFC option.
A Datagram naming a request beyond a known client-initiated stream limit should cause H3_ID_ERROR.
requirements.reason: The public QUIC stream resource intentionally does not expose the peer stream-limit watermark to HTTP/3. The permitted fallback therefore treats an uncreated ID as a future stream and drops it, avoiding a guessed connection close.

requirements.summary: SETTINGS_H3_DATAGRAM accepts only the values zero and one.
An invalid SETTINGS_H3_DATAGRAM value closes the connection with H3_SETTINGS_ERROR 0x109.
QUIC DATAGRAM frames are withheld until both endpoints advertise SETTINGS_H3_DATAGRAM equal to one.
A server accepting HTTP Datagram 0-RTT must not lower its remembered SETTINGS_H3_DATAGRAM value.
requirements.reason: This product never associates HTTP Datagrams or sends its HTTP/3 SETTINGS in 0-RTT. QUIC 0-RTT exists, but the HTTP Datagram feature becomes available only after fresh bidirectional SETTINGS exchange.

requirements.summary: A client storing HTTP Datagram 0-RTT state must validate the fresh setting against the remembered value.
requirements.reason: The resumption store does not retain SETTINGS_H3_DATAGRAM and the client cannot send HTTP Datagrams in 0-RTT, so the conditional stored-setting behavior is unreachable.

requirements.summary: A client detecting an HTTP Datagram setting downgrade after 0-RTT must close with H3_SETTINGS_ERROR.
requirements.reason: HTTP Datagram 0-RTT state is neither stored nor used; negotiation is repeated at 1-RTT before the HTTP Datagram association can exist, leaving no downgrade comparison to perform.

requirements.summary: Implementations supporting HTTP/3 Datagrams should always advertise setting one to reduce fingerprinting.
requirements.reason: The secure product default keeps HTTP Datagrams disabled and advertises zero until the application explicitly opts in. This makes authority and memory allocation explicit at the cost of the RFC fingerprinting recommendation.

requirements.summary: A generic Capsule-aware intermediary should forward Capsules without modification.
requirements.reason: The published MASQUE proxy terminates typed UDP or IP tunnels and does not provide a generic HTTP intermediary or transparent Capsule forwarding mode.

requirements.summary: A generic intermediary should forward unknown Capsule Types without modification.
requirements.reason: No generic transparent Capsule intermediary is exposed. The framing codec preserves unknown values for future adapters, while endpoint MASQUE processing deliberately drops unknown types.

requirements.summary: An endpoint silently drops an unknown Capsule Type and can continue parsing the following Capsule.
Capsule Protocol is unavailable on messages containing Content-Length, Content-Type, or Transfer-Encoding.
Responses using Capsule Protocol never use status 204, 205, or 206.
A receiver treats forbidden Capsule message fields or statuses as malformed rather than establishing the protocol.
Capsule receivers should avoid waiting for an entire Capsule Value before processing it.
requirements.reason: The incremental parser consumes fragmented framing but exposes only complete Capsule values. Retention is strictly bounded by caller-selected Capsule and buffer limits; a streaming value-consumer API remains explicit residual work.

requirements.summary: Capsule processing failures are surfaced as typed malformed or incomplete message failures.
Every recognized Capsule payload contains exactly the fields defined for its registered type.
Recognized Capsule payloads with extra or truncated fields fail as malformed or incomplete messages.
Capsule types carrying redundant internal length fields must verify their consistency.
requirements.reason: RFC 9297 DATAGRAM and the permanently supported MASQUE Capsule payloads contain no redundant internal length field; their single outer Capsule Length is enforced by the shared framing parser.

requirements.summary: A clean stream FIN with a partially retained final Capsule is an incomplete message failure.
Capsule-Protocol is parsed as a Structured Field Item whose bare value is Boolean.
A non-Boolean or multiply occurring Capsule-Protocol field is handled as absent.
Unknown Capsule-Protocol Structured Field parameters do not disable a true Boolean value.
The typed MASQUE response builder never emits Capsule-Protocol on an invalid response status.
Typed MASQUE requests and successful responses include Capsule-Protocol true for intermediary visibility.
An intermediary does not re-encode HTTP Datagrams without identifying Capsule Protocol on the request.
requirements.reason: The product exposes no generic cross-connection HTTP Datagram re-encoder. MASQUE proxy processing terminates one authorized tunnel and therefore cannot enter this forwarding behavior.

requirements.summary: An intermediary should not convert QUIC Datagrams to Capsules when its outgoing connection supports QUIC Datagrams.
requirements.reason: No intermediary forwarding or QUIC-to-Capsule conversion API exists; the typed endpoint adapters select their own delivery mechanism and never translate across connections.

requirements.summary: An intermediary should drop an oversized QUIC Datagram instead of converting it into a reliable Capsule.
requirements.reason: There is no intermediary re-encoding path. Oversized endpoint Datagrams are rejected against the current transport maximum and are never converted to Capsules.

requirements.summary: DATAGRAM Capsule parsing applies extension-specific practical payload limits.
A known unusably large DATAGRAM Capsule is rejected before its declared value can grow retained memory.
A re-encoding intermediary should avoid accumulating a complete Capsule before producing a QUIC Datagram.
requirements.reason: The product does not expose DATAGRAM Capsule to QUIC DATAGRAM intermediary re-encoding, so no re-encoding accumulator or associated flow-control debt exists.

requirements.summary: Published HTTP Datagram extensions use Capsule Protocol so they work across HTTP versions and intermediaries.
Capsule registry submissions must include a short Capsule Type field.
requirements.reason: This is an IANA registry submission rule for registration applicants, not endpoint, proxy, relay, or gateway wire behavior implemented by this product.

requirements.summary: IANA must not assign reserved Capsule Type values of the form 0x29*N+0x17.
requirements.reason: This requirement governs IANA registry allocation rather than runtime behavior. The product neither allocates nor submits Capsule Type registrations.

requirements.summary: IANA must not list reserved Capsule grease values as assigned types.
requirements.reason: This is an IANA registry publication obligation and cannot be performed by an HTTP endpoint or the repository's permanent-codepoint manifest.

requirements.summary: The built-in CONNECT-UDP URI Template uses only simple level-one variable expansion.

The fixed template has an HTTPS scheme, validated nonempty authority, and nonempty default path.
Every generated CONNECT-UDP path starts with the slash-prefixed well-known MASQUE location.
Both supported template variables are expanded only into ordered path segments.
Generated paths always contain the encoded target host followed by the decimal target port.
The non-configurable default template contains no non-ASCII Unicode characters.
Every literal byte in the fixed template lies in the visible ASCII range from 0x21 through 0x7e.
The built-in template uses none of the reserved, fragment, label, path-segment, or path-style expansion operators.
Template validity is guaranteed by construction while authority and variable values are validated before expansion.
Invalid authority or target configuration returns a typed error before any PreparedRequest can be emitted.
A UDP proxy deployment should offer the default well-known template location for generic clients.
Target hosts accept only RFC IPv6address or ASCII reg-name forms and target ports use the required decimal form.
Neither the target host nor the target port can be represented as an empty variable value.
URI Template expansion percent-encodes every colon in a validated raw IPv6 target literal.
Target ports outside the inclusive range from one through 65535 are rejected before request creation.
Request creation expands the validated host and port into the path before returning metadata to an HTTP adapter.
A proxy receiving a DNS target must resolve it before sending a successful HTTP response.

Every non-success response keeps payload unavailable and returns a typed failure from confirmation.

The response builder represents HTTP/1.1 success only as the complete protocol-switch response.
Only status 101 is accepted by the HTTP/1.1 success response builder and client confirmation state.
HTTP/1.1 success generation and validation require a Connection field containing Upgrade.
HTTP/1.1 success generation and validation require one Upgrade field equal to connect-udp.
HTTP/1.1 success generation and validation require a true Capsule-Protocol Structured Field.
Any incomplete or non-101 HTTP/1.1 success handshake returns failure and leaves client payload blocked.
HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 request metadata uses the CONNECT method.
HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 request metadata exposes connect-udp as the Extended CONNECT protocol.

The fixed HTTPS scheme and generated slash path are never empty for HTTP/2 or HTTP/3 requests.
HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 adapters receive the fixed HTTPS scheme contract and already-expanded request path.
The response builder represents HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 success only with a complete Capsule Protocol response.
Every status in the inclusive 200 through 299 range is accepted as Extended CONNECT success.
Extended CONNECT success generation and validation require a true Capsule-Protocol field.
A non-2xx or incomplete Extended CONNECT response returns failure and never unlocks datagram payload.
The stable UDP surface has only the implicitly allocated Context ID zero and exposes no reallocation operation.
An unknown Context ID must be silently dropped or retained only in a short finite registration buffer.
Context ID zero encoding rejects every UDP Proxying Payload longer than 65527 bytes.
Receiving an oversized Context ID zero payload must abort its corresponding request stream.
An oversized UDP datagram carried in a DATAGRAM Capsule should be discarded without buffering its contents.
A datagram arriving before its corresponding request must be silently dropped or buffered for only about one round trip.

requirements.summary: Forwarding should avoid making target-facing UDP traffic more bursty than the received sequence.

requirements.summary: Do not negotiate SSLv2.
requirements.reason: Both OTP option builders allow only TLS 1.3 and TLS 1.2, and the post-handshake version decoder rejects anything else. Live tests exercise both permitted versions, so SSLv2 is unreachable on the applicable HTTP/1.1 and HTTP/2 TLS paths.

requirements.summary: Do not negotiate SSLv3.
requirements.reason: The exact allowlist and post-handshake decoder admit only TLS 1.2 or 1.3. The live permitted-version matrix makes SSLv3 unreachable on both OTP endpoint roles.

requirements.summary: Do not negotiate TLS 1.0.
requirements.reason: The client and server configure only TLS 1.3 and 1.2, and reject any other negotiated version before exposing the stream. Existing live tests cover each allowed version.

requirements.summary: Do not negotiate TLS 1.1.
requirements.reason: The client and server configure only TLS 1.3 and 1.2, and reject any other negotiated version before exposing the stream. Existing live tests cover each allowed version.

requirements.summary: Reviewed obligation: Support TLS 1.2.
requirements.reason: Both OTP endpoint roles explicitly include TLS 1.2, and the independent HTTP/1.1 ALPN fixture completes TLS 1.2 handshakes and exchanges an authenticated request.

requirements.summary: Reviewed obligation: Support TLS 1.3.
requirements.reason: Both OTP endpoint roles explicitly include TLS 1.3, and independent transport and HTTP/1.1 fixtures complete authenticated TLS 1.3 handshakes.

requirements.summary: Prefer TLS 1.3 over earlier TLS versions when TLS 1.3 is implemented.
requirements.reason: The option lists place TLS 1.3 first, but no existing test offers TLS 1.2 and 1.3 simultaneously and observes the selected version in both endpoint roles. OTP negotiation semantics are therefore assumed rather than current-source evidenced.

bounded_verification_task.acceptance_focus: Prove TLS 1.3 wins a simultaneous TLS 1.2/1.3 offer in both endpoint directions.
bounded_verification_task.maximum_scope: One independent dual-version TLS peer fixture and focused client/server tests; no public API change.
acceptance: Offer TLS 1.2 and 1.3 simultaneously to each library-owned OTP endpoint direction.
Assert TLS 1.3 is selected and the test fails if either option builder is reordered or constrained to TLS 1.2.

requirements.summary: When TLS 1.2 is supported, follow every RFC 9325 recommendation that applies to TLS 1.2.
requirements.reason: This is an aggregate obligation. Cipher policy, compression, resumption, renegotiation, record limits, nonce construction, key groups, revocation, and stapling still contain Open findings, so this row cannot close independently.

bounded_verification_task.acceptance_focus: Close only after every applicable TLS 1.2 child row is non-Open with current evidence.
bounded_verification_task.maximum_scope: One generated aggregate gate over the RFC 9325 TLS 1.2 rows.
acceptance: List every applicable TLS 1.2 row transitively required by occurrence 8.
Refuse closure while any listed row is Open or lacks current-source executable evidence.

requirements.summary: A new transport protocol integrating TLS must use only TLS 1.3.
requirements.reason: This occurrence expressly covers new TLS-integrating transports. The QUIC core emits and accepts only the TLS 1.3 SupportedVersions value, rejects any other server selection, and has authenticated handshake tests.

requirements.summary: A newly designed application protocol layered on TLS must integrate TLS 1.2 and TLS 1.3.
requirements.reason: The repository implements standardized HTTP/1.1, HTTP/2, and HTTP/3; it does not define a new application protocol. Existing HTTP version support is governed by those protocol specifications, so this protocol-designer duty has no library-owned triggering state.

requirements.summary: Do not negotiate DTLS 1.0.
requirements.reason: No public client or server API provides DTLS. UDP transport is QUIC, whose TLS 1.3 handshake is expressly outside the RFC 9325 DTLS profile.

requirements.summary: Reviewed obligation: Support DTLS 1.2.
requirements.reason: No public client or server API provides DTLS, so this positive DTLS capability is outside the declared product surface.

requirements.summary: Reviewed obligation: Support DTLS 1.3.
requirements.reason: No public client or server API provides DTLS, so this advisory DTLS capability is outside the declared product surface.

requirements.summary: Prefer DTLS 1.3 when DTLS 1.3 is implemented.
requirements.reason: The antecedent is false because the library implements no DTLS endpoint.

requirements.summary: A TLS 1.2 client must not fall back to an earlier TLS version.
requirements.reason: The client performs one OTP TLS handshake with an allowlist containing only TLS 1.3 and 1.2; it has no retry path that widens the version set. The post-handshake decoder also rejects older versions.

requirements.summary: If a protocol defines both dynamic TLS upgrade and a separate TLS-only method, implementations must support the TLS-only method.
requirements.reason: HTTP in this repository uses cleartext and dedicated TLS listeners/connect paths and exposes no STARTTLS-style in-band upgrade. The conditional protocol shape does not occur.

requirements.summary: Administrators must prefer the separate TLS-only method over dynamic upgrade.
requirements.reason: This is an administrator deployment choice and the library exposes no dynamic-upgrade mode to choose.

requirements.summary: If a protocol has only dynamic TLS upgrade, implementations must expose a strict no-plaintext policy.
requirements.reason: The library implements no protocol whose only protection mechanism is an in-band TLS upgrade, so the antecedent is false.

requirements.summary: Administrators must enable the strict no-plaintext policy for an upgrade-only protocol.
requirements.reason: This is an external administrator duty and there is no upgrade-only protocol mode in the public API.

requirements.summary: HTTP clients and servers intended for the Web must support HSTS.
requirements.reason: The integrated client parses, bounds, persists, expires, applies, and can explicitly configure HSTS. Server responses accept arbitrary header fields, including Strict-Transport-Security. Tests prove verified learning, URI upgrade, and that an upgrade never bypasses certificate authentication.

requirements.summary: A deployed web server should send HSTS unless doing so would weaken security.
requirements.reason: Whether a particular deployment should emit Strict-Transport-Security depends on its certificate and topology. Applications own response headers, while the library already permits the field; automatic emission would invent operator policy.

requirements.summary: TLS 1.2 implementations and deployments should not negotiate TLS-level compression unless the application is proven safe.
requirements.reason: Neither OTP option builder requests compression, but no repository test or pinned OTP capability evidence proves that a non-null TLS 1.2 compression offer is impossible on OTP 28 and 29.

bounded_verification_task.acceptance_focus: Prove null-only TLS compression behavior for both client and server roles.
bounded_verification_task.maximum_scope: One TLS 1.2 wire probe plus one OTP-version capability assertion.
acceptance: Show that the client offers only null compression and the server rejects a non-null-only offer.
Fail on OTP 28 and 29 if TLS compression becomes negotiable.

requirements.summary: When session resumption is used, authenticate and encrypt the resumption information.
requirements.reason: The HTTP server disables legacy session reuse, but the exact TLS 1.2 client cache and TLS 1.3 ticket behavior of the configured OTP versions is not tested. QUIC tickets are authenticated and encrypted, but RFC 9325 Section 5 makes that comparison insufficient for the applicable OTP paths.

bounded_verification_task.acceptance_focus: Determine reachability first; if reachable, prove authenticated and encrypted resumption state.
bounded_verification_task.maximum_scope: Focused OTP TLS 1.2/1.3 session and ticket probes; no QUIC claim and no broad performance suite.
acceptance: Determine separately whether client and server OTP paths resume sessions or issue/use tickets under the exact configured options.
If resumption is reachable, prove authentication, encryption, lifetime, key rotation/destruction, and PSK-DHE behavior; otherwise prove it remains disabled.
Promote any observed ungoverned behavior to an implementation task instead of treating absence of evidence as compliance.

requirements.reason: The custom QUIC ticket uses AES-256-GCM, but QUIC is out of scope here. Current tests do not establish whether applicable OTP TLS emits tickets or which protection it uses.

If resumption is reachable, prove authentication, encryption, lifetime, key rotation/destruction, and PSK-DHE behavior; otherwise prove it remains disabled.
Promote any observed ungoverned behavior to an implementation task instead of treating absence of evidence as compliance.

requirements.reason: The custom QUIC API has an explicit current/previous key ring, but no current-source test establishes applicable OTP TLS ticket issuance or rotation. It is unsafe to infer compliance from the unrelated QUIC key ring.

requirements.summary: A configurable Maximum Segment Lifetime uses one minute as its recommended value.
requirements.reason: The shipped version set is immutable for a listener lifetime and exposes no live fleet-rollout control, so no runtime MSL value is consumed; the centralized policy documents the prerequisite for any future rollout feature.

requirements.summary: Every incompatible Version Negotiation packet includes every version in the server's Offered Versions set.
A client searches the server's Version Negotiation list for a locally supported version.
A client aborts the connection attempt when the server list contains no eligible mutually supported version.
After finding a mutual version, the client selects it and creates a new first flight using that negotiated version.
Client connection machinery never emits a Version Negotiation packet.
A server silently ignores every received Version Negotiation packet without changing handshake phase.
Version compatibility is allowed only for a pair explicitly specified as compatible.
A server performing non-identity compatible negotiation selects a client-listed version that it supports and knows to be compatible.
requirements.reason: The server accepts the supported Chosen Version and performs only the identity transformation; it never proactively changes the client's first flight to another version, so the conditional non-identity selection path is absent.

requirements.summary: A server aborts the handshake if a selected compatible first flight cannot be converted.
requirements.reason: The shipped server performs no non-identity first-flight conversion and therefore has no conversion failure state; supported client-selected v1 and v2 flights are parsed directly under their wire version.

requirements.summary: A document declaring compatibility between versions specifies how clients learn the negotiated version.
requirements.reason: This is a requirement on specifications that publish a new compatibility relationship, not on endpoint runtime behavior; the separately inventoried RFC 9369 defines the v1/v2 relationship.

requirements.summary: Specifications for mutually compatible versions use the same mechanism for communicating the negotiated version.
requirements.reason: This recommendation governs authors of compatibility specifications rather than endpoint execution; this package implements only the single published v1/v2 relationship defined by RFC 9369.

requirements.summary: Negotiated-version handshake validations also apply to a first flight converted from another compatible version.
requirements.reason: The server does not perform a non-identity first-flight conversion; each v1 or v2 first flight is authenticated, decoded, and validated directly under the version carried on that connection.

requirements.summary: The default Original Version policy tries to avoid the extra round trip of incompatible negotiation.
The Original Version and compatible-version advertisement maximize likely server parsing and preferred-version compatibility.
Both endpoints exchange Version Information inside authenticated TLS transport parameters during the handshake.
Client-sent Available Versions always includes the client's Chosen Version.
A client ignores a Version Negotiation packet that contains its Original Version.
Once a client has acted on Version Negotiation, it ignores Version Negotiation packets for the replacement attempt.
Both endpoints parse peer Version Information as a bounded authenticated transport parameter.
Malformed Version Information causes the endpoint to close the connection rather than continue the handshake.
A QUIC v1 Version Information parse failure closes with TRANSPORT_PARAMETER_ERROR code 0x08.
A zero Chosen Version or zero Available Version is treated as a Version Information parsing failure.
A server treats client Version Information as malformed when Chosen Version is absent from Available Versions.
Every supported negotiating QUIC version has a wire-visible VERSION_NEGOTIATION_ERROR close path.
The server validates that the client's authenticated Chosen Version equals the connection's negotiated version.
A client Chosen Version mismatch closes the server connection with VERSION_NEGOTIATION_ERROR.
Over a QUIC v1 connection, a client Chosen Version other than v1 closes with VERSION_NEGOTIATION_ERROR.
A client reacting to Version Negotiation does not complete when authenticated server Version Information is missing, except for the v1 legacy rule.
The client closes when the server's authenticated Chosen Version was absent from the client's Available Versions.
Missing authenticated server Version Information after a Version Negotiation exchange produces VERSION_NEGOTIATION_ERROR, subject to the v1 exception.
A client that acted on Version Negotiation validates the authenticated server Available Versions against its preference order.
The client closes if authenticated server support would have caused it to choose a different negotiated version.
After acting on Version Negotiation, the client rejects an empty server Available Versions list.
The client validates that authenticated server Chosen Version equals the negotiated connection version.
A server Chosen Version mismatch closes the client connection with VERSION_NEGOTIATION_ERROR code 0x11.
Server operators use the specified three-step Offered, Acceptable, and Fully Deployed version rollout sequence.
requirements.reason: This library exposes one immutable supported-version set and no fleet deployment mutation API, so it cannot perform an operator rollout; the centralized policy explicitly records the required MSL-gated design if mutation is added.

requirements.summary: An ALPN token is reused across QUIC versions only when transport features, ALPN support, and explicit compatibility permit it.
The replacement connection after incompatible negotiation performs a fresh ALPN negotiation independent of the Original Version.
Designers of future QUIC versions attempt to preserve compatibility with commonly deployed versions.
requirements.reason: This requirement applies to authors designing a future QUIC version, while this package implements published v1 and v2 and does not define a new version specification.

requirements.summary: A future compatibility document for versions supporting Retry specifies compatible and incompatible negotiation interaction with Retry.
requirements.reason: This is a requirement on a future compatibility document rather than endpoint runtime behavior; this project defines no new QUIC version or compatibility specification.

requirements.summary: TLS session tickets are tightly bound to one QUIC version and are rejected across versions by both endpoints.
A future compatibility document for 0-RTT-capable versions addresses 0-RTT packets in a converted first flight.
requirements.reason: This is a requirement on a future compatibility specification; the server performs no non-identity first-flight conversion and this project does not publish a new QUIC version.

requirements.summary: A client negotiating down to v1 accepts missing server Version Information as the authenticated synthetic value v1 with only v1 available.
Negotiation involving implemented QUIC v2 uses the complete authenticated RFC 9368 mechanism rather than the v1 legacy exception.

requirements.summary: QUIC v2 implements the v1 transport, TLS, and recovery behavior while applying only RFC 9369's version field, packet type, Initial secret, HKDF label, and Retry integrity differences.
An HTTP/3 server accepts both QUIC v1 and v2 so Alt-Svc discovery does not impose needless version negotiation or TCP fallback.
Every endpoint supporting QUIC v2 sends, processes, and validates the authenticated version_information transport parameter.
Endpoints supporting both v1 and v2 should perform compatible negotiation in either direction to avoid an additional round trip.
requirements.reason: The client implements authenticated v1-to-v2 and v2-to-v1 compatible switching, but the server deliberately accepts either original version without proactively converting a first flight; unsupported versions still use bounded incompatible Version Negotiation.

requirements.summary: A server sends Retry with the same original QUIC version carried by the triggering Initial and authenticates it with that version's integrity key.
After accepting Retry, the client sends the token-bearing subsequent Initial on the Retry and original connection version rather than switching versions.
A server that changes to a negotiated version after Retry includes the original destination, initial source, and Retry source connection ID transport parameters needed to authenticate that exchange.
requirements.reason: The server never performs a non-identity compatible switch after Retry; it keeps the triggering Initial's version for Retry and for the accepted token-bearing connection, so this conditional post-Retry switch state cannot occur.

requirements.summary: The server protects every CRYPTO frame using the version selected for that connection, for both v1 and v2 handshakes.
Once the client observes a compatible negotiated version, it rekeys and sends every subsequent Initial using that negotiated version.
A compatibly switching server retains original-version Initial receive keys until it successfully processes a negotiated-version Handshake packet.
requirements.reason: The server does not perform non-identity compatible switching and therefore owns only the Initial keys for the accepted original version; there is no second negotiated-version Handshake transition that could trigger premature original-key discard.

requirements.summary: Both endpoints derive and send Handshake and 1-RTT protection under the negotiated QUIC version.
After version selection, an endpoint drops long-header packets carrying any other version before transport frames can affect connection state.
A compatible switch preserves the original version specifically for 0-RTT packets while Initial, Handshake, and 1-RTT move to the negotiated version.
The client never applies a v1 TLS ticket or paired NEW_TOKEN to a v2 initial connection, or v2 resumption state to a v1 initial connection.
The server authenticates the originating QUIC version of every session ticket, Retry token, and NEW_TOKEN token and rejects use under another version.

standards.title: CUBIC for Fast and Long-Distance Networks

normative_inventory.scope: Atomic uppercase BCP 14 mandatory and advisory clauses; MAY and OPTIONAL are excluded.

requirements.summary: Elapsed CUBIC epoch time excludes intervals where application or flow control prevents window updates.
The Reno-friendly region selects W_est when it exceeds the current CUBIC curve value.
Reno-friendly alpha becomes one once W_est reaches the congestion window saved before reduction.
The concave region increments cwnd by the bounded target-minus-window ratio for acknowledged bytes.
The convex region uses the same bounded per-ACK target-minus-window increment rule.
Packet loss immediately reduces the CUBIC congestion window and slow-start threshold on entering recovery.
Every independent CUBIC congestion response uses the recommended multiplicative factor beta of 0.7.
A cwnd-based implementation prevents congestion-window growth when bytes in flight do not fill cwnd.
The QUIC connection path applies the cwnd-based sparse-flight safeguard before every CUBIC ACK update.
Independent ECN congestion events continue reducing CUBIC until one maximum datagram remains.
Persistent CE at one datagram exponentially reduces pacing rate while retaining one complete send opportunity.
Multi-flow mode shortens W_max with the RFC fast-convergence factor after a lower saturation point.
A known single-CUBIC-flow environment should disable the fast-convergence heuristic.
requirements.reason: The pure controller supports and diagnoses an explicit single-flow mode, but the public runtime has no trustworthy topology signal and currently chooses multi-flow fast convergence by default rather than guessing that an Internet path carries only one flow.

requirements.summary: A TCP retransmission timeout resets W_est to the window at the next congestion-avoidance epoch.
requirements.reason: QUIC has probe timeouts but no TCP retransmission-timeout congestion event; RFC 9438 itself states that QUIC loss is detected only after an acknowledgment, so this TCP-only transition is absent.

requirements.summary: A late optional spurious-loss restoration keeps newer state after cwnd has already exceeded its saved value.
requirements.reason: The optional spurious-fast-retransmit restoration algorithm is not implemented, so there is no saved stale CUBIC state that could overwrite a newer window; ordinary late acknowledgments retain current state.

requirements.summary: CUBIC uses a bounded slow-start algorithm whenever cwnd has not exceeded ssthresh.
The initial CUBIC slow start uses the RFC 9406 HyStart++ delay and Conservative Slow Start states.
The CUBIC curve never uses the inefficient low growth constant C equals 0.04.
The fixed-point curve uses the recommended C equals 0.4 coefficient without floating-point drift.

entries.reason: The rejected proposal would redefine cwnd_prior as flight size; the published definition and RFC 9002 safeguards remain authoritative.

requirements.summary: A client uses a gateway key configuration only after its origin and bytes have been authenticated and integrity protected.
requirements.reason: decode_key_configuration verifies syntax and supported algorithms, but Client accepts the resulting value without any authenticated acquisition proof, trusted gateway identity, or integrity metadata. The caller can therefore supply an unauthenticated but structurally valid configuration, and no test distinguishes authenticated acquisition from attacker-supplied bytes.

requirements.summary: A malformed application/ohttp-keys member invalidates the complete key-configuration collection instead of yielding a recoverable subset.
Any additional field on the client-to-relay request is independent of the encapsulated request content.
requirements.reason: The OHTTP module returns encrypted bytes but does not construct the HTTP POST to the relay and exposes no typed policy for its additional fields. An application can attach content-derived or identifying fields outside this module, and no integrated request test proves independence.

requirements.summary: Every additional client-to-relay field is selected only when the relay will remove it before forwarding toward the gateway.
requirements.reason: forward_request intentionally accepts no inbound header collection, but the library has no integrated client request builder or relay HTTP forwarder that can prove which outer fields were sent and removed. The pure value alone cannot enforce the contract across both HTTP hops.

requirements.summary: The relay forwarding value never adds information outside the gateway identity, required media type, and unchanged encapsulated request.
Information forwarded from a target response is returned to the client only inside an encapsulated response.
requirements.reason: seal_response can encapsulate a caller-supplied binary HTTP response, but the gateway primitive neither sends the target request nor owns the target response and outer gateway response. There is no integration boundary that prevents an application from copying target-derived fields outside the ciphertext.

requirements.summary: A successful gateway response contains only status 200, the response media type, independent fields, and the encapsulated response body.
requirements.reason: forward_response validates only media type and body size and returns bare bytes. It does not construct or validate the status and complete outer header set, so the required minimal HTTP response envelope has no library-owned implementation or executable proof.

requirements.summary: A client never encapsulates a target request carrying an Expect 100-continue expectation.
A gateway generates an error instead of processing a decrypted request that carries an Expect 100-continue expectation.
A relay or gateway receiving an invalid outer OHTTP message returns an HTTP response with a 4xx status code.
requirements.reason: The primitive functions return typed Error values, but no OHTTP HTTP-server adapter maps every invalid media type, size, key, parse, or decryption failure to a finite 4xx response. Unit tests observe errors rather than an HTTP response status.

requirements.summary: Errors found after successful request decapsulation, including target errors, are returned only in an encapsulated response.
requirements.reason: admit_request now retains GatewayContext and encapsulates malformed binary HTTP, Expect, and target-policy failures, but the library still has no target execution adapter that owns target timeouts, resets, or returned errors. Close with a deterministic target fixture proving each post-decapsulation and target failure remains outer 200/message-ohttp-res and decrypts to one bounded inner error.

requirements.summary: Both the client-to-relay request and relay-to-gateway request use authenticated HTTPS.
requirements.reason: relay rejects a non-HTTPS gateway URI, but the module does not represent the relay resource URI or execute either HTTP exchange. It therefore cannot enforce TLS, certificate verification, or HTTPS on the client-to-relay hop, and cannot prove that the accepted gateway URI is the endpoint actually contacted.

requirements.summary: A client authorizes the selected Oblivious Gateway Resource for every target resource it places in an encapsulated request.
requirements.reason: Gateway has a server-side target-authority allowlist, but Client contains no gateway identity, target policy, or authorization callback. A client can seal a binary HTTP request for any authority under any structurally valid public configuration.

requirements.summary: The key configuration selected for request encryption is authenticated and attributable to the intended gateway.
requirements.reason: The public KeyConfiguration value carries no gateway identity or authentication evidence, and client validates only wire shape and supported algorithm identifiers. This repeated security requirement therefore remains unmet for the same acquisition boundary as Section 3.

requirements.summary: Every request uses a newly generated HPKE context and fresh high-quality encapsulation randomness.
A client omits identifying information from the outer relay request unless it trusts the relay to remove that information.
requirements.reason: The module does not build the client-to-relay HTTP request, accept a relay trust policy, or constrain the calling application's fields. The ciphertext primitive cannot prove that authorization, cookies, connection metadata, or other identifiers stay out of the outer request.

requirements.summary: A relay performs its outbound request and inbound response forwarding under the HTTP intermediary forwarding rules.
requirements.reason: forward_request and forward_response validate pure values but never execute HTTP, strip hop-by-hop fields, receive a gateway status, or forward its response. Full RFC 9110 Section 7.6 behavior therefore remains application-owned and untested.

requirements.summary: The relay forwarding contract excludes unknown client fields from the request it prepares for the gateway.
The relay value cannot add client address, connection, credential, or pseudonymous identity information to a forwarded request.
Any relay-generated request information excludes unique permanent client identifiers and pseudonymous client identifiers.
A relay adds forwarding delay only with client consent or awareness.
requirements.reason: The public Relay is an immediate metadata-free forwarding instruction with no delay, batching, scheduler, clock, or timing-policy input, so intentional relay delay is unreachable in this library boundary. Adding any relay delay capability must reopen this row and add a client-awareness contract plus a deterministic clock test.

requirements.summary: A gateway uses an explicit mechanism such as an allowlist to prevent arbitrary target-resource relay abuse.
A separately originated target request does not use an insecure HTTP connection between gateway and target.
requirements.reason: authorize_request already rejects non-HTTPS binary HTTP and the direct test covers an allowed authority with an http scheme, but no target adapter binds that accepted scheme and authority to a certificate-verified connection. Close with TLS, plaintext, wrong-certificate, cross-origin redirect, and address-override fixtures proving only the authenticated HTTPS target receives bytes.

requirements.summary: A gateway ensures that its OHTTP private keys are not valid in any other HPKE protocol using the same request label.
requirements.reason: gateway_key imports caller-provided raw X25519 private bytes without key provenance, purpose binding, or a non-exportable key handle. The same bytes can be passed to another protocol using the label, and no misuse test detects cross-protocol reuse.

requirements.summary: A client or relay automatically retries only after a positive signal that the encapsulated request was not processed or forwarded.
requirements.reason: The module exposes no supervised OHTTP exchange or retry decision API and does not classify REFUSED_STREAM, H3_REQUEST_REJECTED, GOAWAY, interruption, or ambiguous connection failure. Applications must implement the mandatory decision independently and have no executable library oracle.

requirements.summary: A client includes Date in encapsulated requests unless it knows that the gateway does not use Date for anti-replay.
requirements.reason: seal_request accepts caller-authored binary HTTP and has no Date policy, injectable clock, gateway capability signal, or test for omission and inclusion. The finite replay store detects exact ciphertext replay but does not satisfy this client request-authoring recommendation.

requirements.summary: A gateway that uses a Date acceptance window does not rely on that window being secret.
requirements.reason: The shipped Gateway has no Date parser, clock, acceptance window, or Date-conditioned response. Its ReplayStore retains bounded ciphertext fingerprints and makes no secrecy claim about a time window that does not exist in this capability boundary.

requirements.summary: A Date-corrected retry creates a fresh encryption of the changed request using a new HPKE context.
requirements.reason: There is no typed Date correction or OHTTP retry transition. Ordinary seals use fresh HPKE contexts, but no executable state model proves a Date mutation followed by exactly one fresh re-encryption.

requirements.summary: A client performs at most one retry using a gateway-adjusted Date value.
requirements.reason: No Date-retry state or attempt counter exists at the OHTTP API boundary, so callers can retry an adjusted value without a finite library-enforced limit and no test observes the required terminal transition.

requirements.summary: A Date-conditioned gateway error uses no-store or Vary: date so intermediaries do not reuse it incorrectly.
requirements.reason: The gateway primitive does not condition responses on Date and does not construct an outer HTTP error response. There is consequently no Date-conditioned library-owned response to which cache directives can be attached.

requirements.summary: A client uses a gateway-provided Date only for the one corrected retry and never for future requests or other resources.
requirements.reason: The library has no scoped Date value, one-shot retry token, or response-to-request state machine. A caller can retain and reuse a Date value without detection, and no test establishes destruction after one retry.

requirements.summary: A gateway uses HTTPS when forwarding a decrypted request to a target resource on a separate server.
requirements.reason: authorize_request retains and requires the https scheme before a request can be admitted, but no target execution step binds the authority to a certificate-verified connection or prevents redirect and address overrides. Close with paired TLS and plaintext listeners proving only the authenticated TLS target receives the admitted request.

requirements.summary: An application using OHTTP mitigates tracking through unique or small-anonymity-set client configurations.
requirements.reason: Client accepts one caller-selected KeyConfiguration and contains no consistency proof, anonymity-set signal, configuration distribution policy, gateway URI, or relay URI. The library cannot distinguish a widely shared configuration from one minted uniquely for a user.

entries.reason: The reported issue changes only the example HTTP Content-Length from 38 to 35 for the already printed 35-byte encapsulated response; it does not alter the cryptographic format or any library-owned HTTP envelope because this module returns bytes rather than authoring Content-Length.

requirements.summary: A client abandons service access when cryptographically protected service-binding resolution fails through authentication, SERVFAIL, transport failure, or timeout.
requirements.reason: The resolver callback error type is Nil and carries neither DNS protection state nor failure class. refresh_https_records collapses every callback error to Nil and run_https_exchange proceeds with the TCP route, so the implementation cannot distinguish an allowed insecure-resolution fallback from a protected-resolution downgrade that should abort.

entries.reason: The RFC Editor rejected the proposed octal-to-hexadecimal test-vector change: RFC 1035 presentation syntax treats the three decimal digits after the backslash as an octet value, so decimal 210 is correctly encoded as hexadecimal d2. The published vector remains authoritative.

The RFC Editor rejected replacing SHALL with MUST because RFC 2119 defines SHALL and MUST as equivalent absolute requirements. The proposal therefore changes no sender or receiver behavior and the published keyword remains authoritative.

The RFC Editor rejected removing quotes around the port example: every SvcParamValue uses the Appendix A character-string presentation encoding, where quotes are permitted, while the decoded value remains a decimal integer. The published example is valid and creates no new behavior.

requirements.summary: A detected invalid proxy template aborts request construction before any request is sent to the IP proxy.
requirements.reason: No template input can reach connect_ip, so it cannot report which configuration was invalid. validate_scope rejects a small set of target strings before preparing metadata, but there is no transport adapter, no send synchronization point, and no test proving zero network activity for every invalid-template class.

requirements.summary: A proxy deployment that needs broad client interoperability serves CONNECT-IP at the standard default template location.
requirements.reason: connect_ip constructs the client-side default path, but there is no inbound CONNECT-IP listener or route registration API that serves '/.well-known/masque/ip/{target}/{ipproto}/'. Existing HTTP server integration covers CONNECT-UDP and cannot prove that the CONNECT-IP default location is accepted.

requirements.summary: A client derives the request path and query by correctly expanding the configured IP proxy URI Template.
requirements.reason: The fixed default builder percent-encodes supplied target values and wildcards and renders the protocol number, but it is not a general template expansion. It cannot accept a configured template, expand query variables, or enforce the Section 3 template restrictions, so the overall expansion contract remains open.

requirements.summary: Every IP proxying exchange runs over TLS, QUIC encryption, or an equivalent authenticated encryption protocol.
requirements.reason: PreparedRequest stores an authority and selected HTTP version but no authenticated connection or scheme. The pure CONNECT-IP API can be attached to an arbitrary transport by the caller, and there is no live certificate-verification test for an IP tunnel.

requirements.summary: An IP proxy validates decoded target and ipproto variables and resolves a DNS-name target to A and AAAA results before replying.
requirements.reason: There is no inbound CONNECT-IP request parser, target-variable decoder, IP proxy acceptor, or DNS resolver for this capability. validate_scope runs only on the client's pre-encoded IpScope and does not parse RFC 9484 target ABNF or produce address routes before a response.

requirements.summary: The proxy retains every address and route assignment for exactly the lifetime of the open CONNECT-IP request stream.

requirements.summary: If an IP proxy tears down an idle tunnel, it also closes the corresponding request stream.

requirements.summary: Any response outside the successful CONNECT-IP response contract causes the client to abort the request.

standards.title: Shared Brotli Compressed Data Format

requirements.summary: Accept the applicable shared Brotli format, including custom dictionaries and framed streams when offered.
requirements.reason: The public codec does not claim or expose a general RFC 9841 compliant decompressor. DictionaryBrotli is the RFC 9842 dcb profile only: one external raw LZ77 prefix dictionary, an unframed complete stream, and a 16 MiB window ceiling. Serialized/custom dictionaries, the RFC 9841 container, and its other codecs are outside this registered coding boundary rather than partially accepted.

requirements.summary: Emit a valid shared Brotli stream when using the supported raw-prefix dictionary mode.
Use identical dictionary bytes at the compressor and decompressor.
Restrict custom static references to lengths four through thirty-one with a nonzero size-bit entry.
requirements.reason: No custom static dictionary word list can enter the DictionaryBrotli API. Its sole dictionary input is the RFC 9842 raw prefix byte string, so the conditional custom-word reference rules have no reachable representation.

requirements.summary: Require each custom transform index to be below the configured custom transform count.
requirements.reason: No custom transform list or context-dependent static dictionary can enter the DictionaryBrotli API. The raw-prefix profile has no transform index to validate; standard RFC 7932 static transforms are covered by the separate RFC 7932 map.

requirements.summary: Recognize the defined shared dictionary stream structure before resolving its dictionary components.
requirements.reason: RFC 9842 dcb declares its external dictionary to be type raw and treats it as a prefix dictionary. The API accepts exactly those raw bytes and has no serialized-dictionary media type or parser, so the conditional Section 5 structure is outside the advertised profile.

requirements.summary: Validate the extended WBITS field in the inclusive range ten through sixty-two.
requirements.reason: The general RFC 9841 large-window stream mode is not exposed. DictionaryBrotli implements the narrower RFC 9842 dcb profile, whose advertised decoder capability ends at 16 MiB (WBITS 24); accepting WBITS 25 through 62 would expand a capability the public coding does not claim.

requirements.summary: Reject even unused nonzero distance symbols whose maximum decoded distance exceeds two to the power sixty-three minus four.
Reject framed shared Brotli streams whose container version bits are unsupported.
requirements.reason: The RFC 9841 framing container is not an accepted public input format. DictionaryBrotli consumes the distinct RFC 9842 fixed dcb header followed by one unframed complete stream, so no framing-container version is processed.

requirements.summary: Preserve the decoder state across framed chunks that request continuation of the previous stream.
requirements.reason: The RFC 9841 framing container is not an accepted public input format. Each bounded decode call consumes one complete unframed dcb representation, so a keep-decoder chunk and cross-chunk continuation state cannot be requested.

standards.review_scope: All 10 inventoried legacy normative clauses are dispositioned for the exact public capability boundary. The implemented portion is RFC 9842 dcb's unframed raw-prefix stream and its applicable distance checks. General serialized/custom dictionaries, large-window streams above the dcb ceiling, and the framing container are not accepted or advertised and are explicitly NotApplicable; this is a complete map, not a claim of general RFC 9841 codec conformance.

standards.title: Compression Dictionary Transport

requirements.summary: Do not use invalid, regexp-containing, or foreign-origin URL patterns.
requirements.reason: Dictionary admission constructs the bounded eight-component URLPattern against the fetched HTTPS URL and refuses construction errors or regexp groups before storage. Selection reconstructs it against the canonical outbound URL, applies the same-origin check first, and propagates resource exhaustion as a typed error. Focused, full-constructor, independent Node/Chromium, percent-encoding, canonical-host/port, IPv6, cross-origin, and adversarial-budget cases cover the reachable profile.

requirements.summary: Require a match member before accepting a Use-As-Dictionary directive.
An empty match-dest list matches every request destination.
Clients without request-destination support treat match-dest as empty and match all destinations.
requirements.reason: DestinationCapability distinguishes SupportedDestination (including the real empty Fetch destination) from DestinationsUnsupported. select_dictionary_for_request ignores destination lists in both matching and precedence only for unsupported capability. Ordinary regressions preserve origin, partition, freshness, path-length and recency rules and the existing string API. Independent matching and specificity mutations are detected.

requirements.summary: Send a nonempty stored identifier with the advertised hash for that dictionary.
requirements.reason: The integrated http Client never emits Available-Dictionary, Dictionary-ID, dcb, or dcz. The compression module only parses and serializes caller-supplied field values and does not send HTTP requests; therefore the conditional branch in which this library sends Available-Dictionary for a stored record is absent.

requirements.summary: Treat a server dictionary identifier as an opaque string.
Never use the server identifier alone as proof of dictionary contents.
requirements.reason: Neither dictionary codec accepts an identifier as input. Encoding derives the wire hash from the actual dictionary bytes, decoding compares the wire hash with those bytes, and the explicit selected-record policy recomputes the bytes and compares both the stored and advertised hashes before encoding. Identifier-only and stale-ID substitutions are deterministic failures.

requirements.summary: Validate dictionary contents against the dictionary hash before use, independently of an opaque server identifier.
requirements.reason: Both dcb and dcz decode validate the fixed-header SHA-256 value against the supplied bytes before invoking the codec. The selected-record encode policy separately recomputes the content hash and checks it against the stored and single advertised hash; wrong bytes, forged cached hashes, and wrong advertisements fail before encoding.

requirements.summary: Do not use an unknown dictionary type.
Send one Available-Dictionary header containing one selected hash.
requirements.reason: The integrated http Client has no compression-dictionary request negotiation path and never emits Available-Dictionary. serialize_available_dictionary creates one bounded Structured Field Item but does not own or mutate an HTTP header list, so this conditional wire-sending obligation belongs to an application that elects to compose that primitive.

requirements.summary: Select only a fresh dictionary or one explicitly allowed to be served stale.
requirements.reason: The explicit Store adopts the conservative permitted policy of selecting fresh dictionaries only. Admission requires fetched_at < fresh_until in one signed 64-bit caller clock domain; selection requires fetched_at <= now < fresh_until, rejecting future records and the exact expiry boundary. Applications derive and supply the deadline from their cache policy; serve-stale eligibility is intentionally not needed by this stricter subset.

requirements.summary: Select one dictionary, preferring a matching explicit destination over no destination.
Among equal destination candidates, prefer the longest match string.
Among equal destination and match-length candidates, prefer the most recently fetched dictionary.
Echo a stored server-provided dictionary identifier in the outgoing Dictionary-ID header.
requirements.reason: The integrated http Client never selects this standalone Store or emits Dictionary-ID. parse_dictionary_id and serialize_dictionary_id are bounded field-value primitives; an application that elects to send Available-Dictionary owns the conditional request-header composition.

requirements.summary: The outgoing identifier is identical to the decoded stored server identifier.
requirements.reason: The integrated http Client never emits Dictionary-ID. The standalone parser/serializer preserves opaque decoded values but does not own an HTTP request, so there is no library-generated outgoing identifier to compare with a stored server identifier.

requirements.summary: A client advertising dcb can decode resources using windows up to sixteen MiB.
requirements.reason: The public DCB codec accepts a retained Brotli 1.1.0 reference stream whose actual copies reach WBITS 24 distance 16777200, with independently verified output and a payload-free scalar copy trace. The ordinary worker has explicit output/work/window limits and a 256 MiB heap cap. This proves codec capability when budgets admit the resource; automatic HTTP advertisement is a separate capability boundary documented by the NotApplicable negotiation entries.

requirements.summary: A client advertising dcz accepts the dictionary-dependent window floor, capped at 128 MiB.
requirements.reason: Five retained Zstd 1.5.5 sequence-generated streams use actual offsets of 8, 16, 32, 64 and 128 MiB from output back to the first raw-dictionary bytes. Independent decoding and altered/missing-prefix controls verify dependence. Public DCZ decoding matches each independent output with adequate explicit dictionary/output/work budgets; lowering the native streaming window rejects the same bytes. The 128 MiB vector tests decoder cap capability, not encoder permission to emit an equal-to-cap window. Automatic HTTP advertisement is a separate capability boundary documented by the NotApplicable negotiation entries.

requirements.summary: The encoded DCZ window is strictly lower than the RFC dictionary-dependent window limit.
requirements.reason: The public encoder uses fixed compression level 3. Ordinarily executed native regressions inspect the window in the emitted DCZ Zstandard frame for dictionaries at the 8 MiB floor transition and the 128 MiB cap, using input longer than 8 MiB and exact decoded output. Every emitted window is strictly below min(128 MiB, max(8 MiB, 1.25 times dictionary bytes)). Forcing the encoder to emit a larger window makes the retained boundary regression fail; no private FFI level is advertised as a public setting.

requirements.summary: Do not advertise dictionary availability when no eligible dictionary exists or the client chooses not to use one.
requirements.reason: The integrated http Client never advertises dcb or dcz in Accept-Encoding and never emits Available-Dictionary, whether or not an application retains a standalone Store. With no automatic dictionary negotiation option, the forbidden no-match/opt-out advertisement state is unreachable in library-owned request generation.

requirements.summary: Cacheable dictionary-compressed responses vary on Accept-Encoding and Available-Dictionary.
requirements.reason: The server dispatcher has no dictionary registry, content-negotiation option, or dictionary response encoder. compression.encode returns bytes and does not construct an HTTP response. An application that elects to place those bytes in a cacheable response owns Content-Encoding and Vary under the ordinary response API.

requirements.summary: Use compression dictionary transport only in secure HTTPS contexts.
requirements.reason: There is no integrated dictionary transport path in either http Client or Server. The standalone Store additionally accepts and selects only canonical HTTPS origins, while the byte codec has no transport semantics; an application that composes its own CDT exchange must supply authenticated transport policy.

requirements.summary: Drop a response and return an error if any dictionary security mitigation fails.
requirements.reason: The integrated http Client does not negotiate or decode dictionary-compressed HTTP responses, so it has no CDT mitigation pipeline or partially decoded response to deliver. Standalone URL admission/selection and codec calls fail atomically with typed errors, but an application composing them owns its enclosing response-drop policy.

requirements.summary: Clients that restrict response readability apply equivalent protections to dictionary compression.
requirements.reason: The condition is limited to clients, such as browsers, that impose a response-readability and tracking-protection model. This general-purpose HTTP client exposes every received response to its caller and has no browsing context, Fetch response tainting, or CORS readability policy; it also performs no automatic CDT negotiation.

requirements.summary: Use dictionary compression only when both the dictionary and response are fully readable to the protected client.
requirements.reason: The conditional protected-client case is absent: the general-purpose HTTP client has no browser browsing context, response-tainting boundary, or CORS readability model, and it performs no automatic CDT negotiation. Applications that implement such a model must gate their explicit codec composition on both resources.

requirements.summary: Partition and clear dictionaries at least as strictly as cookies.
requirements.reason: The http Client neither owns nor consults compression.Store and never advertises a dictionary. Store is an explicitly application-owned immutable value with partition/profile/all clearing; it is not client cookie state. An application that composes CDT must replace its authoritative Store when its own cookie policy clears and remains responsible for older values it retains.

standards.review_scope: All 26 uppercase BCP 14 clauses are dispositioned against the shipped boundary. Header codecs, HTTPS-only immutable storage and selection, complete supported URLPattern matching, dcb/dcz codecs, and explicit selected-content validation have executable evidence. The integrated HTTP client and server do not advertise, negotiate, or automatically decode compression-dictionary transport; conditional request-header, Vary, response-policy, browser-readability, and cookie-lifecycle duties are therefore explicitly NotApplicable to library-owned behavior rather than represented as partially implemented automation.
